clinicalPearls: Chromosome 14q32 carries an imprinted gene cluster, including DLK1, MEG3 and RTL1, so maternal and paternal uniparental disomy 14 produce two distinct disorders
Maternal UPD14 causes Temple syndrome: pre- and postnatal growth restriction, hypotonia, feeding difficulty, early puberty, and later truncal obesity, resembling Prader-Willi syndrome in infancy
Paternal UPD14 causes Kagami-Ogata syndrome: polyhydramnios, a small bell-shaped thorax with coat-hanger ribs, abdominal wall defects, and developmental delay
The same phenotypes can result from imprinting-centre microdeletions or primary epimutations at 14q32, not only from true uniparental disomy
Uniparental disomy can arise through trisomy or monosomy rescue, so an abnormal prenatal or placental result can be a clue
Diagnosis rests on methylation-specific testing of the 14q32 locus, since karyotype and standard microarray are usually normal
A Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 14 raises the risk of uniparental disomy 14 and should prompt targeted testing
reference.pathophysiology: Uniparental disomy of chromosome 14 occurs when both copies of the chromosome are inherited from one parent. Because 14q32 carries a differentially methylated, imprinted gene cluster, the parental origin determines the outcome: two maternal copies, with loss of the paternally expressed genes, cause Temple syndrome, whereas two paternal copies, with over-expression of paternally expressed genes and loss of maternally expressed ones, cause Kagami-Ogata syndrome. Identical phenotypes can follow imprinting-centre microdeletions or primary epimutations at the same locus, so these disorders are best understood as disturbances of 14q32 imprinting rather than of chromosome number alone.
additionalDifferentials: Prader-Willi syndrome, which Temple syndrome mimics in infancy
Silver-Russell syndrome, for the growth restriction of maternal UPD14
Other imprinting disorders such as Beckwith-Wiedemann and Angelman syndromes
Skeletal or thoracic dysplasia, for the Kagami-Ogata thorax
additionalInvestigations: Methylation analysis of the 14q32 (MEG3/DLK1) differentially methylated region
Microsatellite or SNP analysis to establish uniparental origin and distinguish disomy from deletion or epimutation
Karyotype to detect a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 14
Chromosomal microarray, usually normal but useful to exclude deletions and duplications
Growth, developmental, and endocrine or pubertal assessment
Chest imaging where paternal UPD14 is suspected
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory compromise from a small thorax in Kagami-Ogata syndrome
Severe neonatal feeding difficulty with hypotonia
Precocious puberty in Temple syndrome requiring endocrine management
reference.prognosis: Outlook varies by parental origin: Temple syndrome generally has a fair outcome with growth and developmental support, whereas Kagami-Ogata syndrome carries higher neonatal mortality from respiratory difficulty; both require multidisciplinary follow-up.
pitfalls: Relying on karyotype or microarray, which miss uniparental disomy and epimutations
Not testing for uniparental disomy 14 when a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 14 is found
Confusing Temple syndrome with Prader-Willi or Silver-Russell syndrome without methylation testing
Assuming a normal chromosome number excludes an imprinting disorder
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Cassidy and Allanson's Management of Genetic Syndromes
management: No disease-specific drug therapy exists, so management is phenotype-directed and supportive according to whether Temple or Kagami-Ogata syndrome is present
In Temple syndrome, feeding support and growth monitoring in infancy, suppression of precocious puberty with a GnRH analogue, and later prevention and management of truncal obesity
In Kagami-Ogata syndrome, neonatal respiratory support and ventilation for the small bell-shaped thorax, and surgical repair of abdominal wall defects
Developmental surveillance with early intervention and educational support for delay
Endocrine and growth assessment, with consideration of growth hormone where growth restriction persists
Multidisciplinary follow-up coordinated through clinical genetics with paediatric endocrinology and respiratory input
Genetic counselling based on methylation-specific testing of the 14q32 locus, clarifying the mechanism and recurrence risk, including any Robertsonian translocation
